You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27–40, which are based on Reading
Passage 3 below.
Having a laugh
The findings of psychological scientists reveal the importance of humour
Humans start developing a sense of humour as early as six weeks old, when babies begin to laugh
and smile in response to stimuli. Laughter is universal across all human cultures and even exists
in some form in rats, chimps, and bonobos. Like other human emotions and expressions, laughter
and humour provide psychological scientists with rich resources for studying human psychology,
ranging from the development of language to the neuroscience of social perception.
Theories focusing on the evolution of laughter point to it as an important adaptation for social
communication. Take, for example, the recorded laughter in TV comedy shows. Back in 1950,
US sound engineer Charley Douglass hated dealing with the unpredictable laughter of live
audiences, so started recording his own ‘laugh tracks’. These were intended to help people at
home feel like they were in a social situation, such as a crowded theatre. Douglass even recorded
various types of laughter, as well as mixtures of laughter from men, women, and children. In
doing so, he picked up on a quality of laughter that is now interesting researchers: a simple ‘haha’
communicates a remarkable amount of socially relevant information.
In one study conducted in 2016, samples of laughter from pairs of English-speaking students
were recorded at the University of California, Santa Cruz. A team made up of more than 30
psychological scientists, anthropologists, and biologists then played these recordings to listeners
from 24 diverse societies, from indigenous tribes in New Guinea to city-dwellers in India and
Europe. Participants were asked whether they thought the people laughing were friends or
strangers. On average, the results were remarkably consistent: worldwide, people’s guesses were
correct approximately 60% of the time.
Researchers have also found that different types of laughter serve as codes to complex human
social hierarchies. A team led by Christopher Oveis from the University of California, San
Diego, found that high-status individuals had different laughs from low-status individuals, and
that strangers’ judgements of an individual’s social status were influenced by the dominant or
submissive quality of their laughter. In their study, 48 male college students were randomly
assigned to groups of four, with each group composed of two low-status members, who had just
joined their college fraternity group, and two high-status members, older students who had been
active in the fraternity for at least two years. Laughter was recorded as each student took a turn
at being teased by the others, involving the use of mildly insulting nicknames. Analysis revealed
that, as expected, high-status individuals produced more dominant laughs and fewer submissive
laughs relative to the low-status individuals. Meanwhile, low-status individuals were more likely
to change their laughter based on their position of power; that is, the newcomers produced more

dominant laughs when they were in the ‘powerful’ role of teasers. Dominant laughter was higher
in pitch, louder, and more variable in tone than submissive laughter.
A random group of volunteers then listened to an equal number of dominant and submissive
laughs from both the high- and low-status individuals, and were asked to estimate the social status
of the laugher. In line with predictions, laughers producing dominant laughs were perceived to be
significantly higher in status than laughers producing submissive laughs. ‘This was particularly
true for low-status individuals, who were rated as significantly higher in status when displaying a
dominant versus submissive laugh,’ Oveis and colleagues note. ‘Thus, by strategically displaying
more dominant laughter when the context allows, low-status individuals may achieve higher
status in the eyes of others.’ However, high-status individuals were rated as high-status whether
they produced their natural dominant laugh or tried to do a submissive one.
Another study, conducted by David Cheng and Lu Wang of Australian National University,
was based on the hypothesis that humour might provide a respite from tedious situations in the
workplace. This ‘mental break’ might facilitate the replenishment of mental resources. To test this
theory, the researchers recruited 74 business students, ostensibly for an experiment on perception.
First, the students performed a tedious task in which they had to cross out every instance of the
letter ‘e’ over two pages of text. The students then were randomly assigned to watch a video
clip eliciting either humour, contentment, or neutral feelings. Some watched a clip of the BBC
comedy Mr. Bean, others a relaxing scene with dolphins swimming in the ocean, and others a
factual video about the management profession.
The students then completed a task requiring persistence in which they were asked to guess
the potential performance of employees based on provided profiles, and were told that making
10 correct assessments in a row would lead to a win. However, the software was programmed
such that it was nearly impossible to achieve 10 consecutive correct answers. Participants were
allowed to quit the task at any point. Students who had watched the Mr. Bean video ended up
spending significantly more time working on the task, making twice as many predictions as the
other two groups.
Cheng and Wang then replicated these results in a second study, during which they had
participants complete long multiplication questions by hand. Again, participants who watched the
humorous video spent significantly more time working on this tedious task and completed more
questions correctly than did the students in either of the other groups.
‘Although humour has been found to help relieve stress and facilitate social relationships, the
traditional view of task performance implies that individuals should avoid things such as humour
that may distract them from the accomplishment of task goals,’ Cheng and Wang conclude. ‘We
suggest that humour is not only enjoyable but more importantly, energising.’

passageData.title: Having a laugh
passageData.subtitle: The findings of psychological scientists reveal the importance of humour

paragraphs.text: Humans start developing a sense of humour as early as six weeks old, when babies begin to laugh and smile in response to stimuli. Laughter is universal across all human cultures and even exists in some form in rats, chimps, and bonobos. Like other human emotions and expressions, laughter and humour provide psychological scientists with rich resources for studying human psychology, ranging from the development of language to the neuroscience of social perception.

Theories focusing on the evolution of laughter point to it as an important adaptation for social communication. Take, for example, the recorded laughter in TV comedy shows. Back in 1950, US sound engineer Charley Douglass hated dealing with the unpredictable laughter of live audiences, so started recording his own ‘laugh tracks’. These were intended to help people at home feel like they were in a social situation, such as a crowded theatre. Douglass even recorded various types of laughter, as well as mixtures of laughter from men, women, and children. In doing so, he picked up on a quality of laughter that is now interesting researchers: a simple ‘haha’ communicates a remarkable amount of socially relevant information.

In one study conducted in 2016, samples of laughter from pairs of English-speaking students were recorded at the University of California, Santa Cruz. A team made up of more than 30 psychological scientists, anthropologists, and biologists then played these recordings to listeners from 24 diverse societies, from indigenous tribes in New Guinea to city-dwellers in India and Europe. Participants were asked whether they thought the people laughing were friends or strangers. On average, the results were remarkably consistent: worldwide, people’s guesses were correct approximately 60% of the time.

Researchers have also found that different types of laughter serve as codes to complex human social hierarchies. A team led by Christopher Oveis from the University of California, San Diego, found that high-status individuals had different laughs from low-status individuals, and that strangers’ judgements of an individual’s social status were influenced by the dominant or submissive quality of their laughter. In their study, 48 male college students were randomly assigned to groups of four, with each group composed of two low-status members, who had just joined their college fraternity group, and two high-status members, older students who had been active in the fraternity for at least two years. Laughter was recorded as each student took a turn at being teased by the others, involving the use of mildly insulting nicknames. Analysis revealed that, as expected, high-status individuals produced more dominant laughs and fewer submissive laughs relative to the low-status individuals. Meanwhile, low-status individuals were more likely to change their laughter based on their position of power; that is, the newcomers produced more dominant laughs when they were in the ‘powerful’ role of teasers. Dominant laughter was higher in pitch, louder, and more variable in tone than submissive laughter.

A random group of volunteers then listened to an equal number of dominant and submissive laughs from both the high- and low-status individuals, and were asked to estimate the social status of the laugher. In line with predictions, laughers producing dominant laughs were perceived to be significantly higher in status than laughers producing submissive laughs. ‘This was particularly true for low-status individuals, who were rated as significantly higher in status when displaying a dominant versus submissive laugh,’ Oveis and colleagues note. ‘Thus, by strategically displaying more dominant laughter when the context allows, low-status individuals may achieve higher status in the eyes of others.’ However, high-status individuals were rated as high-status whether they produced their natural dominant laugh or tried to do a submissive one.

Another study, conducted by David Cheng and Lu Wang of Australian National University, was based on the hypothesis that humour might provide a respite from tedious situations in the workplace. This ‘mental break’ might facilitate the replenishment of mental resources. To test this theory, the researchers recruited 74 business students, ostensibly for an experiment on perception. First, the students performed a tedious task in which they had to cross out every instance of the letter ‘e’ over two pages of text. The students then were randomly assigned to watch a video clip eliciting either humour, contentment, or neutral feelings. Some watched a clip of the BBC comedy Mr. Bean, others a relaxing scene with dolphins swimming in the ocean, and others a factual video about the management profession.

The students then completed a task requiring persistence in which they were asked to guess the potential performance of employees based on provided profiles, and were told that making 10 correct assessments in a row would lead to a win. However, the software was programmed such that it was nearly impossible to achieve 10 consecutive correct answers. Participants were allowed to quit the task at any point. Students who had watched the Mr. Bean video ended up spending significantly more time working on the task, making twice as many predictions as the other two groups.

Cheng and Wang then replicated these results in a second study, during which they had participants complete long multiplication questions by hand. Again, participants who watched the humorous video spent significantly more time working on this tedious task and completed more questions correctly than did the students in either of the other groups.

‘Although humour has been found to help relieve stress and facilitate social relationships, the traditional view of task performance implies that individuals should avoid things such as humour that may distract them from the accomplishment of task goals,’ Cheng and Wang conclude. ‘We suggest that humour is not only enjoyable but more importantly, energising.’

questions.prompt: When referring to laughter in the first paragraph, the writer emphasises
questions.evidence: Like other human emotions and expressions, laughter and humour provide psychological scientists with rich resources for studying human psychology, ranging from the development of language to the neuroscience of social perception.

synonymSubstitutions.question: value to scientific research
synonymSubstitutions.passage: provide psychological scientists with rich resources for studying human psychology

distractors.A: Language is only one end of the stated research range, not the main emphasis.
distractors.B: The paragraph says laughter is universal across cultures, not that its principal function is culture.
distractors.D: The passage says laughter exists in some animals, not that it is universal across animal societies.

questions.prompt: What does the writer suggest about Charley Douglass?

options.A: He understood the importance of enjoying humour in a group setting.
options.B: He believed that TV viewers at home needed to be told when to laugh.
options.C: He wanted his shows to appeal to audiences across the social spectrum.
options.D: He preferred shows where audiences were present in the recording studio.

questions.evidence: These were intended to help people at home feel like they were in a social situation, such as a crowded theatre.

synonymSubstitutions.question: enjoying humour in a group setting
synonymSubstitutions.passage: feel like they were in a social situation, such as a crowded theatre

distractors.B: The track created a social atmosphere; the passage does not say viewers needed instructions about when to laugh.
distractors.C: The mixtures of voices concern types of laughter, not appealing across a social spectrum.
distractors.D: He recorded tracks because he disliked the unpredictable laughter of live audiences, so this reverses the passage.

questions.prompt: What makes the Santa Cruz study particularly significant?

options.A: the various different types of laughter that were studied
options.B: the similar results produced by a wide range of cultures
options.C: the number of different academic disciplines involved
options.D: the many kinds of people whose laughter was recorded

questions.evidence: A team made up of more than 30 psychological scientists, anthropologists, and biologists then played these recordings to listeners from 24 diverse societies, from indigenous tribes in New Guinea to city-dwellers in India and Europe. Participants were asked whether they thought the people laughing were friends or strangers. On average, the results were remarkably consistent: worldwide, people’s guesses were correct approximately 60% of the time.

distractors.A: The study used samples from pairs of students; its significance is not a catalogue of laughter types.
distractors.C: Several disciplines participated, but the highlighted result is consistency across societies.
distractors.D: The laughers were English-speaking students; the cultural diversity belonged to the listeners.

questions.prompt: Which of the following happened in the San Diego study?

options.C: Participants who had not met before became friends.
options.D: Some participants were unable to laugh.

questions.evidence: Laughter was recorded as each student took a turn at being teased by the others, involving the use of mildly insulting nicknames.

synonymSubstitutions.question: exchanged roles
synonymSubstitutions.passage: each student took a turn at being teased by the others

distractors.A: The nicknames were mildly insulting; the passage never says anyone became very upset.
distractors.C: The students belonged to fraternity groups; the passage does not report strangers becoming friends.
distractors.D: All students were recorded laughing; inability to laugh is not reported.

questions.prompt: In the fifth paragraph, what did the results of the San Diego study suggest?

options.A: It is clear whether a dominant laugh is produced by a high- or low-status person.
options.B: Low-status individuals in a position of power will still produce submissive laughs.
options.C: The submissive laughs of low- and high-status individuals are surprisingly similar.
options.D: High-status individuals can always be identified by their way of laughing.

questions.evidence: However, high-status individuals were rated as high-status whether they produced their natural dominant laugh or tried to do a submissive one.

synonymSubstitutions.question: can always be identified
synonymSubstitutions.passage: were rated as high-status whether ... dominant ... or ... submissive

distractors.A: Dominant laughs made low-status individuals seem higher in status, so a dominant laugh does not clearly identify actual status.
distractors.B: Low-status individuals in power produced more dominant, not submissive, laughs.
distractors.C: The passage does not say the two groups’ submissive laughs were surprisingly similar.

questions.prompt: each designed to generate a different kind of ___
questions.evidence: The students then were randomly assigned to watch a video clip eliciting either humour, contentment, or neutral feelings.

synonymSubstitutions.question: generate a different kind of
synonymSubstitutions.passage: eliciting either humour, contentment, or neutral feelings

distractors.A: “a kind of laughter” is not what all three videos generated.
distractors.B: “a kind of relaxing” is ungrammatical and describes only one video.
distractors.C: “a kind of boring” is ungrammatical and is not the three-way category.
distractors.D: Anxiety is not the common category generated by the three videos.
distractors.E: “a kind of stimulating” is ungrammatical and does not name the category.
distractors.G: Enjoyment is only one possible feeling, not the general category.
distractors.H: “a kind of amusing” is ungrammatical; amusing describes the humorous video.

questions.prompt: those who had watched the ___ video
questions.evidence: Students who had watched the Mr. Bean video ended up spending significantly more time working on the task, making twice as many predictions as the other two groups.

synonymSubstitutions.question: persisted with the task for longer
synonymSubstitutions.passage: spending significantly more time working on the task

distractors.A: “laughter video” does not identify any of the three clips.
distractors.B: The relaxing dolphin video was not the group that persisted longest.
distractors.C: “boring video” is not one of the described clips.
distractors.D: “anxiety video” is neither grammatical in context nor described.
distractors.E: The evidence identifies the humorous Mr. Bean clip, not a stimulating clip.
distractors.F: “emotion video” is too general and does not select the successful group.

questions.evidence: Cheng and Wang then replicated these results in a second study, during which they had participants complete long multiplication questions by hand. Again, participants who watched the humorous video spent significantly more time working on this tedious task and completed more questions correctly than did the students in either of the other groups.

distractors.A: “laughter task” does not describe hand multiplication.
distractors.B: The multiplication task was tedious, not relaxing.
distractors.D: “anxiety task” is not the task description.
distractors.E: The task was not stimulating; humour had an energising effect afterward.
distractors.H: The task itself was not amusing; the video was humorous.

questions.evidence: ‘Although humour has been found to help relieve stress and facilitate social relationships, the traditional view of task performance implies that individuals should avoid things such as humour that may distract them from the accomplishment of task goals,’ Cheng and Wang conclude.

distractors.A: Humour may cause laughter; it does not reduce laughter.
distractors.B: “reduces relaxing” is ungrammatical and semantically wrong.
distractors.C: “reduces boring” is ungrammatical; boring is an adjective here.
distractors.E: “reduces stimulating” is ungrammatical and reverses the energising effect.
distractors.F: The findings concern emotional effects, but do not say humour reduces emotion generally.
distractors.G: Humour is enjoyable, so it does not reduce enjoyment.
distractors.H: “reduces amusing” is ungrammatical and contradicts humour.

questions.prompt: it may also have a ___ effect on the body and mind
questions.evidence: ‘We suggest that humour is not only enjoyable but more importantly, energising.’

distractors.A: “a laughter effect” does not paraphrase energising.
distractors.B: A relaxing effect conflicts with the emphasized energising effect.
distractors.C: A boring effect is the opposite of energising.
distractors.D: An anxiety effect is not claimed and conflicts with stress relief.
distractors.F: “an emotion effect” is too vague and unnatural here.
distractors.G: Enjoyment is mentioned, but the summary’s “also” targets the more important energising effect.
distractors.H: “an amusing effect” repeats humour’s enjoyable quality, not its effect on body and mind.
